extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of geology and astronomy; educated general readers interested in scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing and forming geological and astronomical hypotheses, emphasizing avoiding premature generalization, using multiple lines of evidence (fossils, observation, analogy), and preferring explanations consistent with known processes and appearances.

rubrics_metrics.name: avoid_premature_generalization
rubrics_metrics.description: That proclivity to generalization which is possessed in greater or less degree by all minds... has unavoidable inconveniences. Through it alone can truth be reached; and yet it almost inevitably betrays into error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not infer universal or absolute propositions from limited experience. Recognize that early sweeping generalizations are often steps toward truer theories, but must be treated as provisional and open to correction as more data accumulate.

rubrics_metrics.name: use_provisional_grouping_as_method
rubrics_metrics.description: Only by provisional grouping can [facts] be brought into such order as to be dealt with; and this provisional grouping is but another name for premature generalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply provisional classifications to organize data for further inquiry, but maintain awareness of their provisional status and be prepared to revise them when contradicted by wider evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: hypotheses_must_harmonize_with_appearances
rubrics_metrics.description: This conclusion harmonizes with the appearances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer hypotheses that fit observed phenomena (e.g., the photosphere/cloud model's agreement with observed solar surface features). Use empirical appearances as a key constraint on acceptable explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: require_internal_physical_consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: If these interior gases are non-luminous from the absence of precipitated matter, must they not for the same reason be transparent? And if transparent, will not the light from the remote side... be nearly as bright as that of the side next to us?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check hypotheses for internal contradictions in their physical consequences (e.g., emission vs. transmission/absorption properties). A plausible mechanism must be consistent in all implied physical effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: prefer_explanations_based_on_known_processes
rubrics_metrics.description: We no longer resort to hypothetical agencies to explain the phenomena displayed by the Earth's crust; but we are day by day more clearly perceiving that these phenomena have arisen from forces like those now at work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor hypotheses that assimilate past causes to processes observed today (uniformitarian thinking) rather than invoking ad hoc, unobserved agencies or sudden catastrophes without explanatory mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: allow_multiple_agencies_rather_than_single_cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of one catastrophic cause, once in universal action, as supposed by Werner... we now recognize several causes, all more or less general and continuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid mono-causal accounts when multiple interacting processes (water action, igneous action, glaciers, coral-builders, micro-organisms) plausibly contributed. Construct explanations that allow combinations and variable dominance of causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: use_analogy_and_direct_observation_to_test_hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: A phenomenon which furnished, by analogy, a verification of the above hypothesis... the cloud ... was obviously much lower than the rest and rudely funnel-shaped... It thus became manifest that the cloud was produced by a feeble whirlwind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ analogies from observed terrestrial phenomena and direct observation to verify or falsify speculative hypotheses (e.g., using a local cloud/whirlwind to support cyclonic origin of sun-spots).

rubrics_metrics.name: avoid_overreliance_on_mineral_characters_for_stratigraphy
rubrics_metrics.description: It is needless here to enumerate the many speculations... These are a few instances of the small trust to be placed in mineral qualities, as evidence of the ages or relative positions of strata.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume lithological similarity implies contemporaneity. Mineral or lithological characters can be misleading; treat them cautiously and corroborate with other evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: prefer_fossil_evidence_over_lithology_for_age_correlation
rubrics_metrics.description: Judged by their fossils, Bala slate and limestone are of the same age as the Caradoc sandstone, 120 miles off.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use fossil content (biostratigraphy) as a more reliable indicator of relative age and correlation across regions than lithological similarity alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: beware_nomenclature_and_classification_bias
rubrics_metrics.description: The original nomenclature of periods and formations necessarily keeps alive the original implications; and the need for arranging new data in some order, results in their being thrust into the old classification, unless their incongruity with it is very glaring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be conscious that historical names and classifications can bias interpretation of new data; resist forcing new observations into old schemes when they conflict—revise classification where warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: value_explanatory_power_across_multiple_traits
rubrics_metrics.description: If this [cyclonic] hypothesis... furnishes an adequate reason for the depression which one of these dark spaces exhibits... Nor are we without some interpretation of the penumbra... there will so be produced that 'thatch'-like aspect which the penumbra presents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer hypotheses that account for multiple independent observed features (e.g., umbra, penumbra, penumbral elongation, 'rice-grain' spots) rather than ones addressing a single trait.

rubrics_metrics.name: use_scale_and_geometry_in_inference
rubrics_metrics.description: The comparative smallness of the light-giving spots and their comparative uniformity of size, show us that they have ascended through a stratum of but moderate depth (say 10,000 miles)... This favours the hypothesis of a molten shell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the sizes, uniformity, and geometry of observed structures to infer physical scales (depth, thickness) and thereby discriminate between competing structural hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: explain_conflicting_traits_by_unifying_mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Considering that they have so many characters in common, it is extremely improbable that their common characters are in some cases the concomitants of vortical motion and in other cases the concomitants of a different kind of action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When apparently conflicting observations occur, prefer explanations that can unify common characters under a single mechanism, and seek mechanisms that explain why some consequences may be unobservable under usual conditions (e.g., vortical motion not always visible in photosphere).

rubrics_metrics.name: recognize_and_correct_past_misleading_inferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Sir R. Murchison shows us, as in the case just cited, that he has himself in past times been misled by trusting to lithological evidence; yet his reasoning all through Siluria shows that he still thinks it natural to expect formations of the same age to be chemically similar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge historical mistakes (e.g., reliance on lithology for age) and actively correct interpretive habits; let demonstrated counterexamples inform changed methodological practice.
